name: Acute Pharyngitis

likely: Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) - when Centor score is high
possible: Fusobacterium necrophorum (consider in older adolescents/young adults with severe symptoms)
pathogens.why: Most pharyngitis is viral. Group A Streptococcus becomes a relevant consideration only with sufficient Centor criteria, and testing (rapid antigen detection or culture) should confirm before treating to avoid unnecessary antibiotic exposure.

investigations.test: Rapid antigen detection test (RADT) or throat culture
investigations.why: Confirms or excludes Group A Streptococcus before committing to antibiotics, directly preventing unnecessary use in viral pharyngitis.

references: IDSA Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis Guidelines
reason: /4 (fever, tonsillar exudate, tender cervical lymphadenopathy, absence of cough) raises probability of Group A Streptococcal pharyngitis. Throat swab/rapid antigen testing is recommended to confirm before committing to antibiotics, per stewardship principles - empiric treatment without testing is discouraged outside high Centor scores with epidemiologic risk.
/4 is low, favoring a viral etiology. Antibiotics are not indicated at this time; testing (rapid strep/throat culture) should guide therapy if clinical suspicion for Group A Streptococcus persists.

clinicalPearls: Sore throat is not synonymous with pharyngitis: it may also arise from submandibular/retropharyngeal/peritonsillar space infections, thyroiditis, gastroesophageal reflux, tumors, or postnasal drainage (Harrison 22e p.300).
Pharyngeal erythema is most commonly seen with viral infection (common cold, influenza), not bacterial disease (Harrison 22e p.300).

Pharyngeal exudate can be mimicked by Candida (cottage-cheese appearance, scrapes off leaving a bleeding surface) or leukoplakia (cannot be scraped off) - do not equate exudate with bacterial pharyngitis (Harrison 22e p.300).
GAS is the only common cause of sore throat that warrants antibiotics; most non-GAS pharyngitis is viral and self-limited (Harrison 22e p.300).
About 10% of adults with sore throat have GAS; in children the prevalence may reach ~35%, peaking at ages 5-15 years, and is higher in winter and early spring (Harrison 22e p.300).

Risk of GAS pharyngitis is elevated in health care and child care workers, teachers, parents of young children, and contacts of known strep cases; clinicians should watch for local outbreaks in military and institutional settings (Harrison 22e p.300).
GAS carriage is common (up to ~20% of schoolchildren, ~5% of adolescents/young adults); rapid antigen tests and culture cannot distinguish true infection from carriage (Harrison 22e p.301).

In adults meeting zero or one Centor criterion, a positive GAS test is very likely a false positive and/or represents carriage; indiscriminate testing of adults with sore throat is discouraged (Harrison 22e p.301).

Lower the threshold to test/treat GAS in patients with a history of acute rheumatic fever, documented strep exposure in the past week, those in a community strep epidemic, and diabetic or immunocompromised patients (Harrison 22e p.301).

In children the Centor criteria are less specific, so GAS pharyngitis should be confirmed by testing; children with pharyngitis but no viral signs (conjunctivitis, runny nose, cough, hoarseness, nonexudative oral lesions) warrant testing (Harrison 22e p.301).
In developed countries the prevalence of rheumatic fever is extremely low, and antibiotic treatment does not prevent poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (Harrison 22e p.300).

Full-blown infectious mononucleosis (EBV) appears in only about one-fourth of cases and is a triad of clinical, hematologic, and serologic findings; new EBV causes 1-6% of pharyngitis in young adults and is rare over age 40 (Harrison 22e p.301).
Heterophil antibody is detectable in only ~40% of mononucleosis patients in the first week but in 80-90% by the third week, so an early negative test does not exclude EBV (Harrison 22e p.302).

Gonococcal pharyngitis is more often asymptomatic than symptomatic; suspect it with persistent sore throat unresponsive to presumptive strep treatment and relevant sexual exposure (Harrison 22e p.302).
Diphtheria produces only mild pharyngitis beneath its characteristic grayish pseudomembrane (Harrison 22e p.302).
Acute HIV infection causes sore throat in roughly half of cases; consider it when sore throat accompanies headache, fever, myalgias, lymphadenopathy, anorexia, and rash (Harrison 22e p.302).
harrison.pathophysiology: Acute pharyngitis (symptoms generally present for days) is most often caused by respiratory viruses; group A beta-hemolytic streptococci (GAS, Streptococcus pyogenes) are a frequent bacterial cause, with other contributors including Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Epstein-Barr virus, HIV, non-group-A streptococci (groups C and G), Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae. Complications of GAS pharyngitis arise from both suppurative spread (e.g., peritonsillar abscess, sinusitis, other invasive GAS infection) and nonsuppurative immune-mediated sequelae (acute rheumatic fever, poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, scarlet fever) (Harrison 22e p.300-301).
additionalDifferentials: Acute infectious mononucleosis (EBV) - marked cervical adenopathy, exudative pharyngitis, palatine petechiae, gelatinous uvula, splenomegaly (Harrison 22e p.301-302)
Non-group-A streptococcal pharyngitis (group C and group G streptococci) (Harrison 22e p.302)
Mycoplasma pneumoniae pharyngitis (persistent sore throat with bronchopulmonary symptoms) (Harrison 22e p.300)
Haemophilus influenzae pharyngitis (cough and otitis media) (Harrison 22e p.300)
infectionMimics: Acute epiglottitis/supraglottitis - sore throat with dysphagia, odynophagia, hoarseness, stridor or tachypnea, drooling; airway emergency (Harrison 22e p.302)
Peritonsillar abscess - fever, dysphagia, profound throat pain with drooling, trismus, 'hot potato voice', unilateral palate bulge and uvular deviation (Harrison 22e p.302)
Retropharyngeal abscess - post-URI in children with sore throat, dysphagia, deep neck pain, neck stiffness, trismus, drooling; severe cases with dyspnea/stridor (Harrison 22e p.302)
Submandibular abscess / Ludwig angina - swelling of the floor of the mouth displacing the tongue posteriorly, usually after dental infection or extraction (Harrison 22e p.302)
Lemierre syndrome - septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein with metastatic infection (Harrison 22e p.302)
Candida pharyngitis - cottage-cheese exudate that scrapes off leaving a bleeding surface (Harrison 22e p.300)
nonInfectiousMimics: Leukoplakia mimicking exudate (cannot be scraped off) (Harrison 22e p.300)
additionalInvestigations: Rapid GAS antigen test: sensitivity ~80%, specificity ~95%; proper technique (swabbing tonsils/pharynx and any exudate or ulceration) is essential to sensitivity (Harrison 22e p.301)
Throat culture: single-swab sensitivity ~85-90%; can be falsely positive in carriers; not recommended for routine adult evaluation given 24-48 h delay (Harrison 22e p.301)
Heterophil antibody test for EBV mononucleosis (low early sensitivity, rises by week 3) (Harrison 22e p.302)
CBC for atypical lymphocytosis in mononucleosis (absolute lymphocytes >4000/uL or relative >50% with >10% atypical morphology) (Harrison 22e p.302)
CT imaging for suspected head and neck abscess (except obvious peritonsillar abscess) (Harrison 22e p.302)
Lateral neck radiograph in epiglottitis may show the 'thumb sign' (not required for diagnosis) (Harrison 22e p.302)
redFlags: Shaking chills/rigors, neck swelling beyond lymphadenopathy, trouble swallowing, drooling, or symptoms persisting >5 days without improvement should prompt urgent re-evaluation (Harrison 22e p.301)
Stridor, dyspnea, hoarseness, or tripod/forward-leaning posture with drooling - suggests epiglottitis and impending airway obstruction (Harrison 22e p.302)
Non-GAS pharyngitis that is not resolving in a teenager/young adult with rigors, neck pain or swelling, or extrapharyngeal symptoms - suspect Lemierre syndrome (Harrison 22e p.302)
Trismus, 'hot potato voice', and unilateral palate bulge with uvular deviation - peritonsillar abscess (Harrison 22e p.302)
Grayish pharyngeal pseudomembrane in a traveler from an endemic area - suspect diphtheria (Harrison 22e p.300, 302)
harrison.prognosis: Both streptococcal and nonstreptococcal pharyngitis should resolve within 3-5 days. Nonsuppurative complications are rare, and even streptococcal pharyngitis is self-limited in the vast majority of cases; outside the U.S., because complications are rare, some guidelines do not recommend routine GAS testing or antibiotic treatment of sore throat (Harrison 22e p.301).
pitfalls: Prescribing antibiotics to the majority of adults with sore throat despite only ~10% having GAS - most cases are viral (Harrison 22e p.300).
Testing adults who meet zero or one Centor criterion: 40-60% of adults with pharyngitis fall here, and a positive test is highly likely to be false-positive or carriage (Harrison 22e p.301).
Relying on throat culture or rapid test to distinguish active infection from GAS carriage - neither can (Harrison 22e p.301).
Applying adult Centor criteria to children, in whom they are less specific (Harrison 22e p.301).
Mistaking Candida or leukoplakia for bacterial pharyngeal exudate (Harrison 22e p.300).
Attempting to examine or swab the posterior pharynx in suspected epiglottitis - this can provoke laryngospasm and should only be done in a controlled setting (Harrison 22e p.302).
Assuming antibiotic treatment of GAS prevents poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis - it does not (Harrison 22e p.300).
A negative early heterophil antibody test does not rule out EBV mononucleosis (Harrison 22e p.302).
harrison.severityClassification: Centor criteria (4 findings, 1 point each): history of fever, absence of cough, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and tonsillar exudate or swelling. For an adult pretest probability of ~10%, post-evaluation probability of GAS is ~2% at 0 points, ~3% at 1, ~8% at 2, ~19% at 3, and ~41% at 4 points (area under the curve 0.79). Conceptually: 0-1 criteria -> neither test nor treat; 2-3 -> rapid antigen test to guide management; 4 -> rapid test or empirical treatment. (Harrison 22e p.300-301).
